A caricaturist is an artist who draws exaggerated portraits of people, usually for humor, entertainment, or to make a sharp point about that person.

But to truly understand what a caricaturist is, you first need to understand what they create, because the two are inseparable.

A caricaturist creates caricatures.

A caricature is a drawing of a real person where their most noticeable physical features — a big nose, a wide forehead, tiny ears, a protruding chin, bushy eyebrows — are deliberately stretched, enlarged, or twisted far beyond what they actually look like in real life.

The magic trick here is this: the drawing looks nothing like a photograph of the person, yet you can recognize the person instantly. That is the skill. A caricaturist doesn't try to draw someone accurately. Instead, they study a person's face, identify the two or three features that make that face unique, and then push those features to an extreme. Everything else in the drawing may be simplified or shrunk down. The result is a distorted, often funny, but immediately recognizable image.

Think of it this way. If someone has a very large forehead, a regular portrait artist would draw it as it is. A caricaturist would draw it so enormous that it takes up half the face — and yet, bizarrely, it would still look more like that person than a careful, realistic drawing might.
What a Caricaturist Does (Their Work and Role)

A caricaturist can work in several different settings and for several different purposes:

1. Entertainment at events
You've likely seen caricaturists at fairs, amusement parks, tourist spots, or birthday parties. They sit with a sketch pad and draw quick, funny portraits of visitors in just a few minutes. People buy these as souvenirs or novelty gifts. The mood here is lighthearted and fun.

2. Political and social commentary
This is where the caricaturist's work becomes genuinely powerful. For centuries, caricaturists have drawn politicians, world leaders, royalty, and other public figures in exaggerated, mocking ways to criticize them, expose their flaws, or ridicule their actions. A politician known for being greedy might be drawn with enormous, grabbing hands. A leader known for arrogance might be drawn with a puffed-up chest a hundred times too large.

This type of caricature appears in newspapers, magazines, and online news platforms. It is a form of satire — using humor and exaggeration to make a serious point or to hold powerful people accountable. In this sense, a caricaturist is not just an artist; they are a social commentator.

3. Illustration and media
Caricaturists also work in editorial illustration, books, advertising, and digital media, creating images of celebrities, athletes, actors, and other well-known public figures.
The Core Skill: What Makes Someone a Caricaturist

The defining skill of a caricaturist is not just the ability to draw. It is the ability to observe and analyze a face — to look at a person and immediately identify what makes their face theirs. This is harder than it sounds.

Once they identify those defining features, they must then decide how much to exaggerate. Too little, and the drawing looks like a clumsy portrait. Too much, and the person becomes unrecognizable. The perfect caricature sits right at the edge — stretched to the point of being absurd, but never losing the essence of the person.

A caricaturist must also understand proportion and composition — knowing that shrinking one feature can make an exaggerated feature stand out even more dramatically. For example, if someone has a large nose, the caricaturist might also draw a very tiny chin to make the nose appear even more dominant.

Caricaturists almost always work with real, recognizable people, particularly:

  • Politicians and heads of state
  • Celebrities, actors, and musicians
  • Athletes
  • Historical figures
  • Members of the public (at events and parties)

Fictional characters are rarely the subject of caricature because caricature depends on the viewer recognizing a real person and understanding the gap between how the person actually looks and how they've been distorted.

The word "caricaturist" can also be used in a broader, non-visual sense to describe anyone — a writer, a filmmaker, a comedian — who presents a one-dimensional, exaggerated, or oversimplified version of a person or idea. For example, you might say that a novelist is being a "caricaturist" if their villain is so purely evil, with no complexity or depth, that the character feels like a cartoon rather than a real human being. In this usage, the word carries a mildly negative tone, suggesting the person is reducing something rich and complex down to just its most obvious, extreme traits.
How a Caricaturist Differs from Other Artists

It helps to briefly contrast a caricaturist with similar types of artists:

A portrait artist aims to capture a person as faithfully and realistically as possible — their exact proportions, their likeness, their dignity. Accuracy is the goal.

A cartoonist creates fictional or stylized characters, often for storytelling purposes. Their characters may not be based on real people at all.

A caricaturist, by contrast, starts with a real person, deliberately abandons accuracy, and uses exaggeration as a tool — either for laughs, for satire, or for both. The distortion is not a mistake or a limitation. It is the art form.

A caricaturist is an artist who specializes in drawing exaggerated, distorted portraits of real people by amplifying their most distinctive physical features. Their work ranges from fun party sketches to biting political commentary published in major newspapers. The best caricaturists are gifted observers who can find the visual "essence" of a person and stretch it to an extreme — producing something that is simultaneously absurd and razor-sharp in its likeness. In a broader sense, the word can describe anyone who reduces a person or idea to its most exaggerated, oversimplified form.
